extendedContent.title: Origins & Mythology
extendedContent.content: Yemojá's origins trace back to the Yoruba people of West Africa, particularly Nigeria. In Yoruba mythology, she is believed to have sprung from Olokun, the primordial ocean. One of the central myths surrounding Yemojá involves her marriage to Òrúnmìlà, the Orisha of wisdom and divination. She birthed many Orisha, solidifying her role as the universal mother. Another prominent myth details her escape from a forced marriage, transforming into a river to evade her pursuers, eventually becoming the ocean. These stories highlight her strength, independence, and transformative power.

extendedContent.title: Role & Significance
extendedContent.content: Yemojá plays a crucial role in the religious and spiritual lives of Yoruba adherents and followers of diaspora religions. She is invoked for blessings related to fertility, childbirth, and family well-being. Her association with the ocean makes her a vital figure for sailors, fishermen, and anyone who depends on the sea for their livelihood. As a mother figure, she is sought for comfort, guidance, and protection. Her devotees often offer her gifts of blue and white beads, seashells, and perfumes. Yemojá represents the nurturing and life-sustaining aspects of water, reminding people of its importance for physical and spiritual health.

extendedContent.title: Symbolism & Interpretation
extendedContent.content: Yemojá's symbolism is rich and multifaceted. Water, her primary element, symbolizes life, purification, and the subconscious. Her association with the ocean represents the vastness of knowledge and the depths of emotions. The color blue is often linked to her, representing the ocean's vastness and tranquility. Fish, as her namesake suggests, symbolize abundance and fertility. Cowrie shells are also a significant symbol, representing wealth, prosperity, and feminine power. Yemojá's image as a strong, maternal figure embodies the strength and resilience of women and the importance of motherhood in Yoruba culture.

extendedContent.title: Legacy & Influence
extendedContent.content: Yemojá's influence extends far beyond West Africa, thanks to the transatlantic slave trade, which carried Yoruba beliefs and practices to the Americas. In Santería (Cuba) and Candomblé (Brazil), she is a major Orisha, syncretized with the Virgin Mary in some traditions. Her image and stories continue to inspire artists, writers, and musicians. She is often depicted in paintings, sculptures, and songs, celebrating her power and beauty. Yemojá has become a symbol of Afro-Caribbean identity and a reminder of the enduring strength of African traditions in the diaspora.

description: Yemojá, also known as Yemonja, is a prominent Orisha (deity) in the Yoruba religion and its diaspora traditions like Santería and Candomblé. She is considered the mother of many Orisha and is strongly associated with the ocean, motherhood, fertility, and healing. Her name is a contraction of "Yeye mo eja", which means "Mother of Fish" in the Yoruba language. Yemojá is often depicted as a powerful and nurturing figure, embodying the life-giving and protective aspects of water. She is venerated as a source of wisdom, strength, and compassion. Myths surrounding Yemojá often involve her role as a protector of women and children, and her ability to provide for her devotees. She is also associated with the moon, reflecting her connection to feminine cycles and intuition. Yemojá's influence extends beyond the physical realm, encompassing spiritual nourishment and emotional well-being.
